stem: A client has low-back pain radiating down one leg with numbness and tingling in a nerve-root distribution. Which condition is most consistent with these findings?

options.A: An isolated lumbar muscle strain, because dermatomal sensory symptoms make nerve-root involvement unlikely.
options.B: Lumbar radiculopathy, which can result from irritation or compression of a lumbar nerve root such as from a herniated disc.
options.C: Acute appendicitis, because unilateral leg paresthesia in a nerve-root distribution is a typical manifestation of appendiceal inflammation.
options.D: Chronic venous insufficiency, because lumbar nerve-root-pattern numbness is a characteristic result of venous reflux.

rationale: Radiculopathy reflects dysfunction of a spinal nerve root and can cause radiating pain, numbness, tingling, weakness, or reflex changes in the affected distribution. Current NCBI StatPearls material on disk herniation notes that lumbar disk herniation can compress adjacent neural structures and produce radiculopathy and sensory disturbances. B is therefore the best match. A does not explain nerve-root-distribution sensory findings, and C and D do not produce this characteristic radicular pattern.
educational_objective: Recognize radiating low-back-to-leg pain with numbness or tingling in a nerve-root distribution as a pattern of lumbar radiculopathy and identify disc herniation as one possible cause.
source_organization: National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI Bookshelf)
source_version_date: Last update September 14, 2025; StatPearls 2026 edition; accessed 2026-08-16
source_locator: Continuing Education Activity — neural compression causing radiculopathy/sensory disturbances; lumbar disk herniation clinical manifestations and nerve-root compression discussion
source_claim_supported: Disk herniation may compress neural structures and cause radiculopathy with radiating pain and sensory disturbances; lumbar nerve-root symptoms can include numbness and tingling.

source_original.stem: A client has low-back pain radiating down one leg with numbness and tingling in a nerve-root distribution. Which condition is most consistent?

options.A: Isolated lumbar muscle soreness because radicular sensory symptoms exclude nerve-root involvement
options.B: Lumbar radiculopathy, often from disc herniation compressing or irritating a spinal nerve root
options.C: Acute appendicitis because unilateral leg paresthesia is a typical manifestation of appendiceal inflammation
options.D: Venous insufficiency because lumbar movement commonly causes dermatomal numbness from venous reflux

source_original.rationale: Sciatica is a clinical pattern of radicular pain that may include numbness, tingling, or weakness along the affected nerve distribution. Lumbar disc herniation is a common cause of nerve-root compression or inflammation.
source_original.source_detail: Clinical presentation and common causes including disc herniation; accessed 2026-08-14.

correction_summary: Replaced the archived lumbosacral-radiculopathy chapter with a current September 2025 NCBI StatPearls disk-herniation source, avoided implying disc herniation is the only cause of radiculopathy, refined distractors, and reduced difficulty from hard to easy.

audit_findings.source_authority: Current NCBI StatPearls; NCSBN 2026 Test Plan
audit_findings.currentness: Source updated 2025-09-14 and published in StatPearls 2026 edition; original NBK430837 is archived.
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final answer says disc herniation is one possible cause rather than universally equating radiculopathy with herniation; pain and sensory findings are directly supported.

distractor_audit.A: A simple muscle strain does not best explain nerve-root-distribution numbness/tingling.
distractor_audit.C: Appendicitis does not characteristically produce dermatomal radicular leg symptoms.
distractor_audit.D: Venous reflux does not produce a lumbar nerve-root sensory distribution.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Other neurologic causes can cause leg paresthesias, but among the listed diagnoses B uniquely matches radiating root-distribution pain and sensory symptoms.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are candidate diagnoses; answer requires recognition of the neurologic pattern.
audit_findings.blueprint: Physiological Adaptation is appropriate for altered neurologic/musculoskeletal function.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked the current 2025 disk-herniation source and broader lumbar-radiculopathy pattern, challenged over-attribution to disc herniation, corrected the wording, and confirmed B remained uniquely correct.
